docs.preview: # Flask Flask is a lightweight [WSGI] web application framework. It is designed to make getting started quick and easy, with the ability to scale up to complex applications. It began as a simple wrapper around [Werkzeug] and [Jinja], and has become one of the most popular Python web application frameworks. Flask offers suggestions, but doesn't enforce any dependencies or project layout. It is up to the developer to choose the tools and libraries they want to use. There are many extensions provided by the community that make adding new functionality easy. [WSGI]: https://wsgi.readthedocs.io/ [Werkzeug]: https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/ [Jinja]: https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/ ## A Simple Example ```python # save this as app.py from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def hello(): return "Hello, World!" ``` ``` $ flask run * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ (Press CTRL+C to quit) ``` ## Donate The Pallets organization develops and supports Flask and the libraries it uses. In order to grow the community of contributors and users, and allow the maintainers to devote more time to the projects, [please donate today]. [please donate today]: https://palletsprojects.com/donate ## Contributing See our [detailed contributing documentation][contrib] for many ways to contribute, including reporting issues, requesting features, asking or answering questions, and making PRs. [contrib]: https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/

report.overview: Flask is the Pallets WSGI web framework — a thin, opinion-light composition layer over Werkzeug (routing, request/response, dev server), Jinja (templating), itsdangerous (signed session cookies), Click (CLI) and Blinker (signals), distributed as the `flask` package plus a `flask` console script. This checkout is the unreleased 3.2.0.dev line on `main`, whose headline change is the merger of `RequestContext` into a single `AppContext`: one context object now carries app, `g`, request, session and URL adapter, is pushed once per request and per CLI command, and is threaded explicitly as a `ctx` first argument through `dispatch_request`, `full_dispatch_request`, `finalize_request`, `preprocess_request`, `process_response` and the teardown methods. The codebase is deliberately split into a sans-IO core (`src/flask/sansio/`) that alternative implementations such as Quart reuse, and IO-bound subclasses (`app.py`, `blueprints.py`) that add WSGI, Click groups and file serving. It targets Python 3.10+, is fully typed (`py.typed`, strict mypy + pyright), and ships its own tutorial, JavaScript and Celery example applications.

system_map.summary: The library entrypoints are the `flask` package namespace (`src/flask/__init__.py` re-exports the public API), the `flask` console script wired to `flask.cli:main`, and `python -m flask` via `__main__.py`. Runtime is split across a sans-IO layer (`Scaffold` → `App` → `Blueprint` in `src/flask/sansio/`) that holds registries and setup logic with no IO, and the IO layer (`Flask`, `Blueprint`, `cli`, `helpers`, `templating`) that performs WSGI dispatch, file serving and server startup. There is no database or persistence layer; the only durable state Flask owns is the signed session cookie written by `SecureCookieSessionInterface`. External integrations are all Pallets-family libraries pinned in `pyproject.toml` dependencies, plus optional `asgiref` (async views) and `python-dotenv` (env files). Build is flit_core; test/lint/type/docs orchestration is tox driven by uv, executed in GitHub Actions.

claims.claim: `src/flask/__init__.py` is the public API surface: 39 explicit `X as X` re-exports covering `Flask`, `Blueprint`, `Config`, the five context proxies, all 10 signals, and the `render_template`/`stream_template` family — nothing is exported implicitly.

The console script is declared as `flask = "flask.cli:main"` under `[project.scripts]`, and `src/flask/__main__.py` is a three-line shim (`from .cli import main; main()`) so `python -m flask` and `flask` share one code path.

The sans-IO boundary is documented in-tree: `src/flask/sansio/README.md` states the folder must do no IO, must not be on a likely IO path, and must not use the Flask globals — which is why `sansio/app.py` declares `default_config` and `response_class` as bare annotations and lets `Flask` in `app.py` supply them.

Class hierarchy is `Scaffold` (shared route/handler registration, static folder, `find_package`) → `App` (config, url_map, blueprints dict, extensions dict, template filters/tests/globals) → `Flask` (WSGI, Click group, sessions, file serving); `Blueprint` follows the same sansio → IO split.

All context state lives in one `AppContext` object holding `app`, `g`, `url_adapter`, `_request`, `_session`, `_flashes` and `_after_request_functions`, stored in the single `ContextVar` `_cv_app` declared in `globals.py`; there is no second request-level ContextVar.

The five public proxies (`app_ctx`, `current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session`) are all `werkzeug.local.LocalProxy` instances over the same `_cv_app`, differing only by attribute name and unbound-error message (`_no_app_msg` vs `_no_req_msg`).

The only persistence layer is the signed cookie: `SecureCookieSessionInterface` builds a `URLSafeTimedSerializer` with salt `"cookie-session"`, hmac key derivation, lazily-resolved SHA-1 digest, and the `TaggedJSONSerializer` payload serializer.

Runtime dependencies are exactly six Pallets-ecosystem packages (blinker≥1.9.0, click≥8.1.3, itsdangerous≥2.2.0, jinja2≥3.1.2, markupsafe≥2.1.1, werkzeug≥3.1.0) with `async` (asgiref) and `dotenv` (python-dotenv) as optional extras.

Build backend is `flit_core>=3.11,<4` with `[tool.flit.module] name = "flask"`, and the sdist explicitly bundles `docs/`, `examples/`, `tests/`, `CHANGES.rst` and `uv.lock` while excluding `docs/_build/`.

Developer commands are tox environments: `tox run` (pytest per Python version), `-e style` (pre-commit all files), `-e typing` (mypy then pyright), `-e docs` (`sphinx-build -E -W -b dirhtml docs docs/_build/dirhtml`), plus `tests-min` and `tests-dev` which pip-install pinned-minimum and git-main dependency sets respectively.

CI is four GitHub Actions workflows: `tests.yaml` (12-way matrix incl. 3.15, free-threaded 3.14t, Windows, Mac, PyPy, min and dev deps, plus a separate mypy/pyright `typing` job), `pre-commit.yaml`, `publish.yaml` (tag-triggered `uv build` → draft GH release → PyPI trusted publishing), and `zizmor.yaml` for Actions security analysis.

Docs are Sphinx `dirhtml` built by Read the Docs using an asdf-installed uv and the `docs` dependency group; 34 top-level doc pages exist including `lifecycle.rst`, `appcontext.rst`, `reqcontext.rst` and `web-security.rst`.

Deployment shape for the library itself is a wheel/sdist on PyPI; the framework's own "deployment" surface for users is `run_simple` from Werkzeug, explicitly documented as development-only in `run_command`'s help text.

feature_catalog.summary: As a framework, Flask's user-facing features are its decorator registries, its CLI subcommands, and its request/response conveniences. Route registration spans `@route` plus seven method shortcuts including the newly added `@app.query` for HTTP QUERY; class-based views come via `View`/`MethodView`. The `flask` CLI ships `run`, `shell` and `routes` built in, discovers app-provided commands through `app.cli`/`blueprint.cli`, and loads third-party commands from the `flask.commands` entry point group. Response handling covers strings, bytes, dicts, lists, generators, tuples, WSGI callables and Response objects; JSON is routed through a swappable `JSONProvider`. Sessions, flashing, file sending, streaming, signals and blueprint nesting round out the surface.

claims.claim: Seven HTTP-method route shortcuts are generated through `Scaffold._method_route`: `get`, `query`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch` (plus `route`); `query` is new in 3.2 for the HTTP QUERY method and is also listed in `views.http_method_funcs`.

`flask run` exposes `--host/-h` (default 127.0.0.1), `--port/-p` (5000), `--cert`/`--key`, `--reload/--no-reload`, `--debugger/--no-debugger`, `--with-threads/--without-threads`, `--extra-files` and `--exclude-patterns`, and inserts `--debug` as its first parameter after definition.

`flask shell` builds an interactive REPL banner from `current_app.import_name` and `instance_path`, honours `PYTHONSTARTUP`, wires `rlcompleter.Completer` against the shell context rather than `__main__`, then calls `code.interact`.
`flask routes` supports `--sort` over `endpoint|methods|domain|rule|match` and `--all-methods`, hides HEAD/OPTIONS by default, and renders a padded ASCII table computed from per-column max widths.

The root CLI group is `FlaskGroup`, which registers three eager options in order (`--env-file`, `--app`, `--debug`) so dotenv loading happens before app import, and sets `auto_envvar_prefix="FLASK"` so every option is also settable via `FLASK_*` env vars.

App discovery supports four forms: explicit `module:name`, `module:factory(args)` with `ast.literal_eval`-parsed arguments, auto-detection of `app`/`application`/`create_app`/`make_app`, and implicit `wsgi.py` then `app.py` in the CWD.

`Flask.make_response` accepts str/bytes/bytearray, any iterator (streaming), dict and list (auto-JSON via `self.json.response`), `BaseResponse` subclasses, arbitrary WSGI callables, and 2- or 3-tuples of `(body, status)`, `(body, headers)` or `(body, status, headers)`.

Class-based views: `View.as_view` supports `init_every_request=False` for a shared instance, applies `cls.decorators` in order, and copies `methods`/`provide_automatic_options` onto the generated function; `MethodView.__init_subclass__` auto-derives `methods` from defined handler names and falls back from HEAD to GET.

Message flashing writes `session["_flashes"]` via a read-append-reassign pattern (deliberately not `setdefault`, so external session backends stay in sync) and emits the `message_flashed` signal; `get_flashed_messages` caches into `app_ctx._flashes` so repeat calls in one request are stable.

Ten Blinker signals are defined in one namespace: template-rendered, before-render-template, request-started, request-finished, request-tearing-down, got-request-exception, appcontext-tearing-down, appcontext-pushed, appcontext-popped and message-flashed.

Async views are opt-in: `ensure_sync` returns plain functions unchanged and wraps coroutine functions via `async_to_sync`, which imports `asgiref.sync.async_to_sync` and raises "Install Flask with the 'async' extra" if asgiref is missing.

Config can be populated six ways: `from_envvar`, `from_prefixed_env` (JSON-decoded `FLASK_*` vars with `__` nesting), `from_pyfile` (exec'd as a module), `from_object` (uppercase attrs only), `from_file` (pluggable loader, text or binary) and `from_mapping`; `get_namespace` extracts prefixed subsets.

Three runnable example apps ship in-repo: `examples/tutorial` (flaskr — sqlite blog with auth blueprint, `init-db` CLI command, 4 test modules), `examples/javascript` (fetch/jQuery/XHR templates) and `examples/celery` (`celery_init_app` subclasses `Task` to push an app context around every job).

`jsonify` and the module-level `flask.json.dumps/dump/loads/load` all delegate to `current_app.json` when an app context is active, falling back to stdlib `json` otherwise, so provider swaps apply globally.

data_flow.summary: Input boundaries are the WSGI environ, the process environment (`FLASK_*`, dotenv files), config files, and the request cookie jar. A WSGI environ becomes a `Request` in `AppContext.from_environ`, which also stamps `request.json_module = app.json` so body JSON decoding uses the app's provider. The `AppContext` is the single state owner for the duration of a request: it holds `g`, the lazily opened session, the bound `MapAdapter`, collected `after_this_request` callbacks and cached flashes. Output boundaries are the `Response` returned to the WSGI server, the `Set-Cookie` session header written in `process_response`, rendered template strings, and log records emitted to `wsgi.errors` or stderr. Config flows one way: `default_config` → `Config` dict → `ConfigAttribute` descriptors (`app.testing`, `app.secret_key`, `app.permanent_session_lifetime`) and per-request property lookups on `Request`/`Response`.

claims.claim: The environ→Request transform happens in `AppContext.from_environ`, which constructs `app.request_class(environ)` and immediately assigns `request.json_module = app.json`, so `request.get_json()` uses the app's JSON provider rather than stdlib json.

The URL adapter is built in `AppContext.__init__` (not at push time) via `app.create_url_adapter`, and any `HTTPException` raised there is stashed on `request.routing_exception` instead of propagating.

`create_url_adapter` applies `TRUSTED_HOSTS` to `request.trusted_hosts` and then recomputes `request.host` through `werkzeug.wsgi.get_host` before binding — host validation happens on this path, before routing.

Session data flows cookie → `SecureCookieSessionInterface.open_session` → `URLSafeTimedSerializer.loads(val, max_age=PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME)` → `SecureCookieSession`; a `BadSignature` silently yields a fresh empty session rather than an error.

Session writes are deferred to `process_response`, which calls `save_session` only when `is_null_session` is false, and `save_session` adds `Vary: Cookie` whenever `session.accessed` is set, deletes the cookie when an emptied session is modified, and otherwise gates on `should_set_cookie`.

Session values are serialized by `TaggedJSONSerializer`, which round-trips non-JSON Python types through single-key tag dicts — ` di` (dict), ` t` (tuple), ` b` (base64 bytes), ` m` (Markup), ` u` (UUID), ` d` (http-date datetime).

Config resolution order is `default_config` copy → `DEBUG` overwritten from `get_debug_flag()` (the `FLASK_DEBUG` env var) → `Config(root_path, defaults)`, with `root_path` swapped to `instance_path` when `instance_relative_config=True`.

Env-file input precedence is: variables already in `os.environ` win, then `-e/--env-file`, then `.env`, then `.flaskenv` — implemented by merging dicts in that order in `load_dotenv` and skipping keys already present in `os.environ`.

Per-request body limits read through `current_app.config` at access time rather than being copied onto the request: `max_content_length`, `max_form_memory_size` and `max_form_parts` each check a private override, then fall back to `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` / `MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE` (500_000) / `MAX_FORM_PARTS` (1_000).

Template context is assembled in `update_template_context`: app-level then reversed blueprint-level context processors run, and the caller's explicit `render_template(**context)` values are re-applied last from a saved copy so they always win.

The default template context processor replaces the `request` and `g` proxies with concrete objects for speed but deliberately leaves `session` as a proxy, because touching it would set `session.accessed` and force a `Vary: Cookie` header.

`send_file`/`send_from_directory` funnel through `_prepare_send_file_kwargs`, which injects `environ`, `USE_X_SENDFILE`, `response_class`, `_root_path` and defaults `max_age` to `app.get_send_file_max_age` before delegating to Werkzeug.

Log output is routed by the `wsgi_errors_stream` LocalProxy: inside a request it writes to `request.environ["wsgi.errors"]`, otherwise `sys.stderr`; `create_logger` attaches `default_handler` only when no handler in the chain already covers the effective level.

Blueprint registration is a data-merge step, not a live delegation: `_merge_blueprint_funcs` copies the blueprint's error handler spec, view functions, before/after/teardown lists, url defaults, url value preprocessors and template context processors into the app's dicts under the dotted name.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows dominate: application construction, WSGI request dispatch, and CLI invocation. Construction is `Flask.__init__` → `App.__init__` → `Scaffold.__init__`, ending with an auto-registered static route that holds only a weakref to the app. Request dispatch is `__call__` → `wsgi_app` → `AppContext.push` (session open, then routing) → `full_dispatch_request` → `preprocess_request` → `dispatch_request` → `finalize_request` → `process_response` (session save) → `ctx.pop` (teardowns). CLI invocation is `main` → `FlaskGroup.make_context` (sets `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI`) → eager `--env-file`/`--app` callbacks → `ScriptInfo.load_app` → command body with an app context pushed via `ctx.with_resource`.

claims.claim: Startup: `Flask.__init__` calls `super().__init__` (App → Scaffold), creates `self.cli = cli.AppGroup()` named after the app, then — if `has_static_folder` — asserts `bool(static_host) == host_matching` and registers `f"{static_url_path}/<path:filename>"` with a `weakref.ref(self)` closure to avoid an app↔view reference cycle (issue #3761).

Startup: `App.__init__` resolves `instance_path` (rejecting relative paths), builds `config` via `make_config`, instantiates `aborter`, `json_provider_class(self)`, the empty `blueprints`/`extensions` dicts, `url_map_class(host_matching=...)`, and sets `_got_first_request = False`.

Request: `Flask.__call__` → `wsgi_app(environ, start_response)` creates the context with `self.request_context(environ)`, pushes it, dispatches, and in `finally` restores it for the debugger via `environ["werkzeug.debug.preserve_context"]` before `ctx.pop(error)`.

Request: `AppContext.push` increments `_push_count`, returns early if already pushed, sets `_cv_app`, sends `appcontext_pushed`, then opens the session via `_get_session()` *before* calling `match_request()` — ordering that lets custom URL converters read the session.

Request: `full_dispatch_request` sets `_got_first_request = True` (freezing setup methods), sends `request_started`, runs `preprocess_request`, short-circuits to `finalize_request` if a `before_request` returned non-None, otherwise calls `dispatch_request`, catching exceptions into `handle_user_exception`.

Request: `preprocess_request` runs `url_value_preprocessors` for `(None, *reversed(req.blueprints))` first, then `before_request_funcs` in the same order — app-level before blueprint-level, outermost blueprint first.

Request: `dispatch_request` raises any stored `routing_exception` through `raise_routing_exception`, returns `make_default_options_response` for automatic OPTIONS, and otherwise calls `ensure_sync(self.view_functions[rule.endpoint])(**view_args)`.

Request: `process_response` runs `ctx._after_request_functions` (from `after_this_request`) first, then app+blueprint `after_request_funcs` in reverse registration order over `chain(request.blueprints, (None,))`, then saves the session.

Teardown: `AppContext.pop` decrements `_push_count`, returns while still nested, then under `_CollectErrors` runs `do_teardown_request`, `request.close()`, `do_teardown_appcontext`, resets the ContextVar, sends `appcontext_popped`, and finally re-raises collected errors as a `BaseExceptionGroup` on Python 3.11+.

Error path: `handle_exception` sends `got_request_exception`, re-raises when `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` (defaulting to `testing or debug`) is truthy, otherwise logs, wraps in `InternalServerError(original_exception=e)`, looks up a 500 handler, and finalizes with `from_error_handler=True` so response-processing failures are logged rather than raised.

Error handler lookup in `_find_error_handler` tries (specific code, then None) × (each blueprint name, then None), walking `exc_class.__mro__` at each step — so a blueprint handler for a specific code beats an app handler for that code, which beats class-based handlers.
CLI: `FlaskGroup.make_context` sets `os.environ["FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI"] = "true"` so a stray module-level `app.run()` becomes a no-op that prints a red warning instead of blocking the command.

CLI: `FlaskGroup.get_command` loads `flask.commands` entry points, prefers built-ins, then calls `ScriptInfo.load_app()` and pushes an app context with `ctx.with_resource(app.app_context())` before delegating to `app.cli.get_command` — which is why `@with_appcontext` is unnecessary for app-registered commands.

CLI: `ScriptInfo.load_app` splits the import path on `r":(?![\\/])"` (so Windows drive letters survive), calls `prepare_import` to insert the package root into `sys.path[0]`, then `locate_app`, and finally sets `app.debug = get_debug_flag()` when `set_debug_flag` is on.

Streaming: `stream_with_context` builds a generator, advances it once with `next()` to capture and push the current `AppContext` (which bumps `_push_count`), yields the user's chunks inside `with ctx:`, and closes a wrapped WSGI iterator in `finally`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is pytest-only, rooted at `tests/` with `testpaths = ["tests"]` and `filterwarnings = ["error"]` so any unexpected warning fails the suite — a notable constraint given 3.2's new deprecation warnings. 22 test modules totalling ~7.6k lines cover the framework, with `test_basic.py` (1974 lines, 95 tests), `test_blueprints.py` (1115) and `test_cli.py` (703) dominating. Fixtures in `conftest.py` provide `app`, `client`, `app_ctx`, `req_ctx`, plus two autouse guards: `_standard_os_environ` clears FLASK_* env vars, and `leak_detector` asserts no app context is left pushed at test end. Static typing is treated as a test surface of its own: `tests/type_check/` holds three assertion-free modules checked by strict mypy and pyright in a dedicated CI job. Coverage is configured with branch mode over `flask` and `tests`, but no coverage gate is enforced in any workflow.

claims.claim: pytest config is minimal and strict: `testpaths = ["tests"]` with `filterwarnings = ["error"]`, so every warning — including the new `RequestContext`/`should_ignore_error` DeprecationWarnings — must be explicitly expected by a test.
`tests/conftest.py` defines an autouse `leak_detector` that pops every still-pushed `app_ctx` after each test and asserts the leak list is empty — a hard guard against context-management regressions.

The autouse `_standard_os_environ` fixture monkeypatch-deletes `FLASK_ENV_FILE`, `FLASK_APP`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI` and `WERKZEUG_RUN_MAIN` so CLI tests can't leak environment state into each other.

The shared `app` fixture builds `Flask("flask_test", root_path=os.path.dirname(__file__))` with `TESTING=True` and `SECRET_KEY="test key"`, which is why `tests/templates/` and `tests/static/` resolve as the app's template and static folders.

Test weight is concentrated: `test_basic.py` 1974 lines / 95 test functions, `test_blueprints.py` 1115, `test_cli.py` 703 / 34 tests, `test_templating.py` 532 — versus 28 lines for `test_session_interface.py` and 21 for `test_subclassing.py`.

CLI tests are backed by fixture apps under `tests/test_apps/`, including `cliapp/factory.py`, `cliapp/multiapp.py`, `cliapp/importerrorapp.py`, a nested `inner1/inner2/flask.py` shadowing case, and `helloworld/wsgi.py` for implicit discovery — plus checked-in `.env` and `.flaskenv` files.

Async coverage is gated on the optional extra: `tests/test_async.py` begins with `pytest.importorskip("asgiref")` and exercises async views, async `View.dispatch_request`, async `MethodView` handlers and async error handlers across app and blueprint.

Type checking is a first-class test target: `tests/type_check/` contains `typing_route.py`, `typing_app_decorators.py` and `typing_error_handler.py`, and both mypy (`strict = true`, `files = ["src", "tests/type_check"]`) and pyright run over them in the `typing` tox env and a dedicated CI job.

The test matrix is unusually broad: CPython 3.10–3.15 including free-threaded `3.14t`, Windows and macOS runners, PyPy 3.11, a minimum-dependency env pinning exact lower bounds, and a dev env installing six Pallets libraries from git main tarballs.

Coverage is configured (branch mode, `source = ["flask", "tests"]`, `exclude_also` for TYPE_CHECKING blocks and `raise NotImplementedError`) but no workflow runs coverage or enforces a threshold — the tox commands invoke plain `pytest -v --tb=short`.

Example apps carry their own tests: `examples/tutorial/tests/` has four modules (auth, blog, db, factory) plus `data.sql` seed data, and `examples/javascript/tests/test_js_example.py` exists — but neither is in `testpaths`, so CI never runs them.
Session security behaviour has direct tests — SameSite attribute variants and `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` key rotation are asserted in `test_basic.py` around lines 342–420.

Test harness code being tested is itself shipped: `FlaskClient.session_transaction` opens a real request context, mutates the session, saves it and re-injects `Set-Cookie` into the client jar, and `FlaskCliRunner.invoke` defaults `obj` to `ScriptInfo(create_app=lambda: self.app)`.

Style enforcement runs via pre-commit (ruff check + ruff format, uv-lock, codespell, merge-conflict/debug-statement/whitespace hooks) with all revs pinned to frozen SHAs, executed both as the `style` tox env and the `pre-commit.yaml` workflow.

risk_map.summary: Flask's security-sensitive surface is narrow but load-bearing: signed session cookies, host validation, file serving, template autoescaping, and code that executes user-supplied Python. The largest structural risk in this checkout is the 3.2 context merge and the `ctx`-first-parameter signature change, which is backstopped only by a signature-sniffing `__init_subclass__` shim that mutates the base `Flask` class at subclass-definition time. Config loading (`from_pyfile`), the shell command (`PYTHONSTARTUP`), and CLI app discovery (`--cert` import strings, factory `ast.literal_eval`) all evaluate code or import arbitrary modules by design. Several defaults are permissive by intent and must be set by deployers: `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=False`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE=None`, `SECRET_KEY=None`, `TRUSTED_HOSTS=None`.

claims.claim: `Flask.__init_subclass__` mutates global class state: when it detects an old-signature override it calls `setattr(Flask, method.__name__, add_ctx(base_method))` on the *base* class, so one legacy subclass anywhere in the process rewraps `Flask`'s methods for every app in that process.
`Config.from_pyfile` compiles and `exec`s the target file into a synthetic module namespace — arbitrary code execution by design, so config paths must never come from untrusted input.
`flask shell` executes `PYTHONSTARTUP` via `eval(compile(f.read(), startup, "exec"), ctx)` before the REPL starts, inheriting whatever that env var points at.

`CertParamType.convert` falls back to `werkzeug.utils.import_string(value, silent=True)` for `--cert`, so a non-path `--cert` value imports an arbitrary dotted module attribute looking for an `ssl.SSLContext`.

`find_app_by_string` parses `module:factory(args)` with `ast.parse` and `ast.literal_eval` — literal-only, so it resists arbitrary expression injection — but `locate_app` still `__import__`s the module, executing it fully.

`open_resource` and `open_instance_resource` join user-supplied `resource` onto `root_path`/`instance_path` with plain `os.path.join` and no `safe_join`, so an absolute or `..` path escapes the directory — safe for the intended developer-controlled use, unsafe if fed request data.
By contrast `send_from_directory` explicitly documents and delegates to Werkzeug's `safe_join`, and the docstring warns that the `directory` argument itself must never come from the client.

Security-relevant defaults ship permissive: `SECRET_KEY=None`, `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS=None`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=False`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE=None`, `TRUSTED_HOSTS=None`, `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH=None` — with no secret key, `get_signing_serializer` returns None and sessions silently degrade to `NullSession`.
Session cookie signing defaults to SHA-1 HMAC via `_lazy_sha1`, deferred to runtime specifically so FIPS builds without SHA-1 can fail at configure time rather than import time.
`open_session` swallows `BadSignature` and returns an empty session, so tampered or key-rotated-out cookies are indistinguishable from no cookie at the application layer — no signal is emitted.

Teardown error handling changed to collect-then-raise: `_CollectErrors.raise_any` raises a `BaseExceptionGroup` on Python 3.11+ but only `self.errors[0]` on 3.10, so identical failures surface as different exception types across supported versions.

Dead/stale developer config: `.devcontainer/on-create-command.sh` runs `pip install -r requirements/dev.txt`, but no `requirements/` directory exists — the repo moved to uv dependency groups in `pyproject.toml`, so devcontainer creation fails.

Deprecated-but-live code paths that must be kept working through 4.0: module-level `__getattr__` shims for `flask.ctx.RequestContext` and `flask.globals.request_ctx`, and the `should_ignore_error` hook checked on every first request in `full_dispatch_request` and again in `wsgi_app`'s finally block.

Blast-radius hotspot: `src/flask/app.py` (1628 lines) and `src/flask/sansio/app.py` (1013 lines) together hold dispatch, error handling, URL building, response coercion and every registration method — nearly every behavioural change lands in one of these two files.

Fragile coupling to Werkzeug internals: `create_url_adapter` comments that it must call `get_host` itself "until bind_to_environ does", and forces `subdomain` to the default because "Werkzeug doesn't implement subdomain matching yet" — both break silently if Werkzeug changes.

`Blueprint.get_send_file_max_age` and `send_static_file` are acknowledged duplicates of the `Flask` methods ("Note this is a duplicate of the same method in the Flask class"), so fixes must be applied in two places.

extension_points.summary: Flask is built almost entirely out of swap points. Class-level attributes on `App`/`Flask` (`request_class`, `response_class`, `json_provider_class`, `config_class`, `app_ctx_globals_class`, `url_rule_class`, `jinja_environment`, `aborter_class`, `session_interface`, `test_client_class`) let subclasses replace nearly every collaborator. Registration flows through `@setupmethod`-guarded decorators that append into dicts keyed by blueprint name or `None`. Third-party CLI commands load from the `flask.commands` entry point group; extensions stash state in `app.extensions[name]`. The JSON layer has two independent extension seams: `JSONProvider` for request/response JSON and `JSONTag`/`TaggedJSONSerializer.register` for session payload types.

claims.claim: Swappable classes are declared as plain class attributes and instantiated lazily: `aborter_class`, `jinja_environment`, `app_ctx_globals_class`, `config_class`, `json_provider_class`, `url_rule_class`, `url_map_class`, `test_client_class`, `test_cli_runner_class`.

Hook factories are explicitly designed for override: `make_config`, `make_aborter`, `create_jinja_environment`, `create_global_jinja_loader`, `create_url_adapter`, `auto_find_instance_path`, `select_jinja_autoescape`, `make_shell_context`, `ensure_sync`, `async_to_sync`.
Third-party CLI commands plug in through the `flask.commands` entry point group, loaded once by `FlaskGroup._load_plugin_commands` before any built-in or app command lookup.
Extensions store per-app state in `app.extensions`, keyed by the extension module's short name — the celery example demonstrates the convention with `app.extensions["celery"] = celery_app`.
JSON behaviour is swapped by subclassing `JSONProvider` (implement `dumps`/`loads`; `dump`, `load` and `response` have defaults) and setting `json_provider_class` or assigning `app.json` directly.

Session payload types extend via `JSONTag` subclasses registered with `TaggedJSONSerializer.register(tag, force=..., index=...)`; the module docstring walks through adding an `OrderedDict` tag at index 0.

Session storage backends plug in by subclassing `SessionInterface` (implementing `open_session`/`save_session`, which raise `NotImplementedError` in the base) and assigning `app.session_interface`; `null_session_class` and `should_set_cookie` are also override points.

The registries new handlers append into are all name-keyed dicts on `Scaffold`/`App`: `view_functions`, `error_handler_spec`, `before_request_funcs`, `after_request_funcs`, `teardown_request_funcs`, `url_value_preprocessors`, `url_default_functions`, `template_context_processors`, with `None` meaning app-level.

`@setupmethod` wraps every registration decorator with `_check_setup_finished`, which raises an `AssertionError` once `_got_first_request` is true — so extensions must complete registration before the first request.

Custom CLI groups are supported end-to-end: `AppGroup.command` auto-wraps callbacks in `with_appcontext` (disable with `with_appcontext=False`) and `AppGroup.group` defaults nested groups to `AppGroup`; `FlaskGroup(create_app=...)` builds a bespoke script entrypoint.

Blueprint CLI grouping is a three-way switch in `Blueprint.register`: `cli_group=None` merges commands into `app.cli` flat, the `_sentinel` default nests them under the blueprint name, and an explicit string nests them under that name.

Template extension points: `template_filter`, `template_test`, `template_global` (usable with or without parentheses as of 3.2) on the app, mirrored by `app_template_filter`/`app_template_test`/`app_template_global` on blueprints, plus `DispatchingJinjaLoader._iter_loaders` for custom template discovery.
URL building failures are extensible through `app.url_build_error_handlers`, a list consulted by `handle_url_build_error`; functions returning None or re-raising `BuildError` are skipped.
Blueprints can be nested arbitrarily via `Blueprint.register_blueprint`, with `register` composing parent and child `url_prefix` and `subdomain` and threading `name_prefix` to produce dotted names.
Deferred setup is available for extensions that need the app object later: `Blueprint.record` / `record_once` append callbacks that receive a `BlueprintSetupState` at registration time.

agent_handoff.summary: Read the sans-IO README first — it defines the hardest rule in this repo: nothing in `src/flask/sansio/` may do IO or touch the Flask globals, so context-dependent code belongs in `app.py`/`blueprints.py`. This is the 3.2 development line, so the second thing to internalise is that `RequestContext` no longer exists as a distinct class and that dispatch-related `Flask` methods take `ctx: AppContext` as their first parameter. Every user-visible change needs a `CHANGES.rst` entry with a `:pr:`/`:issue:` reference and a `.. versionadded:: 3.2` / `.. versionchanged:: 3.2` directive in the docstring — this is followed consistently throughout the codebase. Verify with `tox run -e py3.13` (or plain `pytest`), `tox run -e typing`, and `tox run -e style`; `filterwarnings = error` means a new warning without a matching test will break the suite.

claims.claim: Read first, in order: `src/flask/sansio/README.md` (the IO boundary rule), `src/flask/ctx.py` (the merged `AppContext`), `src/flask/app.py` `wsgi_app`/`full_dispatch_request` (the dispatch spine), and `docs/lifecycle.rst` (the maintainers' own narrative of setup → serving → request).

Safe edit boundary: code in `src/flask/sansio/` must not import `flask.globals` or perform IO; if a change needs `current_app`, `request` or the filesystem, it belongs in the IO subclass in `src/flask/app.py` or `src/flask/blueprints.py`.

Trap: if you add or change a `Flask` dispatch method, it must take `ctx: AppContext` as the first parameter after `self`, or `__init_subclass__`'s signature sniffing will treat subclass overrides as legacy and silently rewrap base-class methods.
Trap: `filterwarnings = ["error"]` turns every warning into a test failure — any new `DeprecationWarning` must be paired with a test that expects it.
Convention: every public change gets a `CHANGES.rst` bullet under the unreleased version with a `:pr:` or `:issue:` role, as the 3.2.0 section demonstrates for all 13 current entries.

Convention: docstrings carry Sphinx `.. versionadded::` / `.. versionchanged::` directives naming the exact release — e.g. `select_jinja_autoescape` documents the 3.2 case-insensitivity change and `do_teardown_request` documents the 3.2 all-callbacks change.

Tests to run: `pytest` (or `tox run` for a specific Python), `tox run -e typing` for mypy+pyright, and `tox run -e style` for the full pre-commit set; docs changes need `tox run -e docs`, which builds with `-W` so any Sphinx warning fails.

Style is enforced by ruff with `select = ["B", "E", "F", "I", "UP", "W"]` and isort configured `force-single-line = true`, `order-by-type = false` — every import is on its own line throughout `src/`, matching that setting.

Typing is strict and non-optional: `[tool.mypy] strict = true` over `src` and `tests/type_check`, plus pyright in basic mode; the package ships `src/flask/py.typed`, so any missing annotation is a public-API regression.

Shared return/callback types live in `src/flask/typing.py` (`ResponseReturnValue`, `ResponseValue`, `HeadersValue`, `AppOrBlueprintKey`); extend these rather than inlining unions, and note `ResponseValue` deliberately includes `AsyncIterable` for Quart's benefit.
Trap: `Blueprint.get_send_file_max_age` and `Blueprint.send_static_file` duplicate the `Flask` versions by design — a fix in one must be mirrored in the other.
Trap: registration methods are frozen after the first request by `@setupmethod`/`_check_setup_finished`, so any new registration API must be decorated with `@setupmethod` to stay consistent.
Trap: `conftest.py`'s autouse `leak_detector` fails any test that leaves a context pushed — when adding context manipulation, make sure pushes and pops balance even on the error path.
Dependency changes require regenerating `uv.lock` — the `uv-lock` pre-commit hook and the `update-requirements` tox env (`uv lock -U`) both enforce it, and the lock file is bundled into the sdist.

Don't add new runtime dependencies casually: the six pinned runtime deps are all Pallets-maintained, and optional features (async, dotenv) are gated behind extras with graceful `ImportError` handling at the call site.

report.agent_prompt:
You are working on **Flask** (pallets/flask), the Python WSGI web framework, at the unreleased **3.2.0.dev** line on `main`. It is a library, not an application: the deliverable is the `flask` package plus a `flask` console script (`[project.scripts] flask = "flask.cli:main"`).

**Architecture.** All source lives in `src/flask/` (~9.5k lines across 20 modules). The defining structural decision is a sans-IO split. `src/flask/sansio/` holds `Scaffold` → `App` → `Blueprint`: registries, setup logic, config handling, template filter/test/global registration — and, per `src/flask/sansio/README.md`, this code **must not do IO and must not use the Flask globals**, because Quart and other alternative implementations reuse it. The IO layer is `src/flask/app.py` (`Flask(App)`, 1628 lines), `src/flask/blueprints.py`, `cli.py`, `helpers.py`, `templating.py`, `testing.py`, `wrappers.py`, `sessions.py`, `json/`.

**The 3.2 change you must internalise.** `RequestContext` has been merged into `AppContext` (`src/flask/ctx.py`). A single `AppContext` now owns `app`, `g`, `url_adapter`, `_request`, `_session`, `_flashes` and `_after_request_functions`, lives in one ContextVar `_cv_app` (`src/flask/globals.py`), and is pushed once per request and per CLI command. All five public proxies (`current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session`, `app_ctx`) are `LocalProxy` views over that one var. `flask.ctx.RequestContext` and `flask.globals.request_ctx` survive only as module-level `__getattr__` deprecation shims removed in 4.0. Correspondingly, `Flask.dispatch_request`, `full_dispatch_request`, `finalize_request`, `preprocess_request`, `process_response`, `handle_*_exception`, `log_exception`, `make_default_options_response`, `do_teardown_request` and `do_teardown_appcontext` now take **`ctx: AppContext` as the first parameter after `self`**. `Flask.__init_subclass__` sniffs subclass signatures and wraps old-style overrides with a DeprecationWarning — if you add or rename one of these methods, keep the `ctx` parameter or you will silently trip that shim.

**Request trace.** `__call__` → `wsgi_app` → `request_context(environ)` (`AppContext.from_environ` builds the `Request` and sets `request.json_module = app.json`) → `ctx.push()` (sets ContextVar, sends `appcontext_pushed`, opens the session, *then* routes via `match_request`) → `full_dispatch_request` (sets `_got_first_request`, sends `request_started`, `preprocess_request`, `dispatch_request`) → `finalize_request` → `make_response` → `process_response` (after_request funcs in reverse, then `session_interface.save_session`) → `ctx.pop(error)` (teardowns under `_CollectErrors`, which raises a `BaseExceptionGroup` on 3.11+ but only the first error on 3.10).

**CLI trace.** `FlaskGroup` (`cli.py`) registers eager `--env-file`, `--app`, `--debug` options in that order, sets `auto_envvar_prefix="FLASK"`, and sets `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI=true` in `make_context` so a stray `app.run()` no-ops. `ScriptInfo.load_app` resolves `module:name`, `module:factory(args)` (literal args only, via `ast.literal_eval`), auto-detected `app`/`application`/`create_app`/`make_app`, or `wsgi.py`/`app.py`. Built-ins are `run`, `shell`, `routes`; plugins load from the `flask.commands` entry point group.

**Conventions.** Every public change needs a `CHANGES.rst` bullet under the unreleased version with `:pr:`/`:issue:`, and a `.. versionadded:: 3.2` / `.. versionchanged:: 3.2` in the docstring. Imports are one-per-line (ruff isort `force-single-line = true`). Typing is strict mypy + pyright over `src` and `tests/type_check`; the package ships `py.typed`.

**Verify with** `pytest` (or `tox run`), `tox run -e typing`, `tox run -e style`, `tox run -e docs`. Two traps: `filterwarnings = ["error"]` fails the suite on any unexpected warning, and the autouse `leak_detector` fixture in `tests/conftest.py` fails any test that leaves an app context pushed.

**Known rough edges.** `Blueprint.get_send_file_max_age`/`send_static_file` are acknowledged duplicates of the `Flask` versions. `create_url_adapter` contains two comments about compensating for Werkzeug gaps (`get_host`, subdomain matching). `.devcontainer/on-create-command.sh` still references a deleted `requirements/dev.txt`. `open_resource`/`open_instance_resource` use plain `os.path.join` (no `safe_join`) and are only safe for developer-controlled paths.
